# The Leaving Moon

The Moon is leaving us.

Not quickly. At about 3.8 centimeters a year—roughly the speed your fingernails grow—it is the slowest departure you will never notice. But the direction is not in doubt, and neither is the evidence, because we asked the Moon directly.

In 1969, the astronauts of Apollo 11 set up a suitcase-sized array of corner-cube mirrors on the Sea of Tranquility, aimed back at Earth. Two more arrays followed on later missions. Observatories have been firing laser pulses at those mirrors ever since. The light goes out, strikes the reflectors, and comes home about two and a half seconds later—a round trip of nearly half a million miles, timed so precisely that we can pin the Moon's distance to within a millimeter. The mirrors still work. Nothing has knocked them over. There is no wind.

Here is the strange part: the Moon is not drifting off due to some lingering recoil from its creation. It is being pushed. And the pusher is us.

The Earth turns once a day; the Moon takes a month to orbit. Because our planet spins faster than its companion circles, the tidal bulge the Moon raises in our oceans gets dragged slightly ahead of the Moon's position. That forward-leaning bulge has gravity, and its gravity tugs on the Moon, giving it a small continuous boost—adding orbital energy, letting it climb to a higher, slower orbit. Every push has a price. The Earth pays in spin: braked by the very tides it flings ahead, our day lengthens by about two milliseconds every century. In effect, the rotational energy of our planet is being handed up to the Moon, dollar by dollar, and the Moon spends it on altitude.

We can check the old ledgers. Certain corals lay down fine daily growth lines within annual bands—a clock inside a calendar. Devonian corals, 370 million years old, record about 400 days per year. The year hasn't changed. The days were shorter, each one about 22 hours long. The Devonian reef-dwellers lived slightly faster lives than we do, on a world spinning slightly quicker beneath them.

Go back further and the Moon crowds the sky. It was likely born in violence—a Mars-sized body striking the young Earth and splashing a ring of debris into orbit, which congealed into the Moon, hovering then at a fraction of its present distance. For a long stretch of deep time it must have hung enormous and low, dragging tides of a scale our coastal charts would treat as satire, across a planet still warm from the collision. It has been climbing away ever since. Four and a half billion years of retreat, and we arrived late enough in the process to mistake it for furniture.

And yet we are lucky in a way so specific it feels personal. The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon—and also about 400 times farther away. Geometry therefore performs a small miracle: the two disks match. When the Moon's orbit crosses the Sun's path precisely enough, the Moon covers the Sun exactly, edge to edge, and a shadow sweeps across the Earth faster than sound. Under that shadow the temperature drops, birds go quiet or go home, a strange 360-degree twilight glows on every horizon at once, and the sky's one impossibility appears: the corona, the Sun's outer atmosphere, otherwise invisible, suddenly blazing around a hole in the day.

This is not a law of physics. It is a coincidence, and it has an expiration date.

Because orbits are ellipses, the Moon is sometimes nearer to us and sometimes farther. When an eclipse occurs while the Moon is at the far end of its range, its disk falls short of the Sun's and we get an annular eclipse—a ring of fire, daylight leaking around the rim. Annular eclipses already slightly outnumber total ones. The average Moon is getting smaller in our sky by the year, at fingernail speed. Somewhere around 600 million years from now, by most estimates, the geometry will fail for good: no more totality, ever. The corona will go unmasked until the Sun itself changes character. Anyone around for the last one will attend an event with no sequel.

We tend to assume the sky is the permanent thing and we are the temporary thing. The Moon's slow exit suggests otherwise. Permanence is a matter of which clock you consult. Mountains are fleeting to geology; species are fleeting to biology; and even the tidy alignments of the heavens are fleeting to astronomy—a limited engagement that happened to be running when we bought our tickets.

But consider the length of the run. Some hundreds of millions of years remain—long enough, probably, to hold every human life that will ever be lived, with seats to spare. No one who reads this, and no one descended from anyone who reads this, needs to check the Moon's ticket for expiration. The window is so wide it functions, for all human purposes, as a permanent feature of the world. We live inside a coincidence the way fish live inside water: unaware, and unharmed by the fact that the water, too, is technically leaving.

There is something oddly tender in the mechanism itself. The Moon recedes because the Earth embraces it—because our spinning world seizes the tides and hurls them ahead, and the Moon, receiving the gift, rises. We slow down so that it can climb. The departure is not theft from outside; it is an exchange between the two oldest partners in the neighborhood.

So stand in the path of totality once, if you can manage it. You will be standing inside the Moon's goodbye as it passes over your upturned face—a shadow cast by something leaving, at a speed you will never feel. It has been taking its leave for four billion years, and it is nowhere near done. Indeed, the farewell will never be completed; long before the Moon finishes going, the Sun will bring the whole scene to a close. The goodbye will be interrupted—which may be the kindest way for anything to end: still in progress, a disk of borrowed light still exactly covering its source, when the lights go out.

The prompt asks me to write freely about whatever I want for 1000 words. This is an open-ended creative writing request. There's no harmful content here, no trick, just an invitation to write.

What should I write about? I have complete freedom here. Let me think about what would make for genuinely interesting, engaging writing. Options:

1. A personal essay about something I find fascinating
2. A short story
3. A reflection on consciousness, AI, existence
4. Something about the natural world
5. A meditation on a small, overlooked thing
6. An exploration of an idea

I think the best approach is to write something that feels genuinely alive and thoughtful—not a canned essay, not a listicle, but real prose with a voice. Let me consider what would actually be interesting.

Some ideas that intrigue me:
- The phenomenology of waiting rooms
- How maps lie
- The strange intimacy of handwriting
- Memory and how it rewrites itself
- The concept of "sonder"—the realization that every passerby has a life as vivid as your own
- Time perception
- The ocean's twilight zone
- What it's like to be a reader vs. a writer
- The history of a single ordinary object

Let me pick something I can write about with genuine texture and surprise. I'm drawn to writing about something ordinary made strange—defamiliarization is one of the great powers of essayistic writing. 

Actually, let me think about what would be most compelling. I could write about:

Option A: An essay on the intimacy of strangers—the sonder idea, but done well, not just naming the neologism. Exploring the moments when we glimpse the interiority of others.

Option B: A meditation on night—the fact that darkness used to be total and now it's optional, and what we lost.

Option C: Something about language itself—how words are fossils, how etymology reveals buried worlds.

Option D: A piece about the moon—how it's drifting away from us, how it used to look bigger, how eclipses are a cosmic coincidence that won't last.

Option E: A piece on the phenomenology of forgetting names mid-conversation, or the tip-of-the-tongue phenomenon.

Option F: Something more personal-feeling—an essay about what it might be like to be me, an AI writing this, without being navel-gazing or cliche.

Option G: The history and strange life of a single thing—like the color blue before humans could make it, or the smell of rain (petrichor), or the pause in music.

Hmm. Let me think about which one I could execute most beautifully in roughly 1000 words.

The moon one (D) has genuinely fascinating facts: the Moon is receding at about 3.8 cm per year (measured by laser ranging via retroreflectors left by Apollo missions); billions of years ago it appeared much larger in the sky and days were shorter (around 6 hours in the early Earth); total solar eclipses are possible only because the Moon currently appears almost exactly the same size as the Sun—a coincidence that will end as the Moon recedes; eventually there will be no more total solar eclipses. Also the tides are slowing Earth's rotation. This is a beautiful piece: the Moon as a clock that's running down, a coincidence we happen to live inside. There's poignancy: we live in the brief era when eclipses work. That's a strong essay with a natural emotional arc: wonder → intimacy → melancholy → a kind of consolation.

The night one (B) is also rich: before artificial light, night was a second world; people experienced "second sleep"—segmented sleep with a waking period in between documented by historian Roger Ekirch; the Milky Way was visible to everyone; light pollution now hides the stars from a large fraction of humanity; blue light and circadian disruption. Also poignant: we colonized the dark and lost something. This has a similar arc.

The strangers one (A) is more philosophical and could feel more like navel-gazing if not handled well, but done right it could be moving.

Let me draft the moon essay in my head:

Opening: something arresting. Maybe start with the fact that the Moon is leaving. "The Moon is leaving us." Then unpack: 3.8 centimeters a year, about the rate fingernails grow. We know this because astronauts left mirrors on the surface and we bounce lasers off them. That detail is wonderful—sniper-precise laser pulses, photons returning after 2.5 seconds.

Then: what the Moon's departure means. Tides are the mechanism—tidal friction transfers Earth's rotational momentum to the Moon, pushing it outward while slowing our spin. So days used to be shorter. In the deep past, a day might have been 6 hours; coral fossils show growth lines recording days per year— Devonian corals show ~400 days per year. That's a great concrete detail: fossils as calendars.

Then the eclipse coincidence: the Sun is 400 times wider than the Moon and also 400 times farther away, so they appear the same size. Total solar eclipse—the Moon exactly kisses the Sun's disk, revealing the corona. But this is temporary. The Moon's disk is shrinking in our sky (angularly) as it recedes; in some hundreds of millions of years, no total eclipses—only annular, ring-of-fire ones. Actually annular eclipses already outnumber total ones now because of the Moon's elliptical orbit. So we live in the window when totality is possible. We happen to exist in the brief age of eclipses.

Then maybe: what this means philosophically. We treat the sky as permanent, the one fixed thing. Even mountains erode, but the Moon seems eternal. Yet it's in motion, a slow leak. Everything is transitory even at the scale of the sky. And yet—the consolation: the timescale is so vast that every human who will ever live could live and die and the eclipse would still work. The recession is roughly: at 3.8 cm/year, to double the Moon's distance (~384,000 km) would take ~10 billion years. But the Sun becomes a red giant in ~5 billion years, and total eclipses end much sooner—estimates vary, maybe 600 million years or so when the Moon can no longer fully cover the Sun. So the window is hundreds of millions of years. Plenty of time.

Emotional close: something about how we live inside coincidences without noticing; the eclipse is a gift of geometry that has an expiration date no human will ever need to check. Or: the Moon as a slow goodbye, but so slow it functions as a presence. "It isn't leaving us, exactly. It's keeping pace with our loss." Hmm.

Also could include: the laser reflectors and that the Moon has no atmosphere so the footprints and the mirrors persist; the retroreflectors still work; some experiments suggest dust is covering them slightly. Also the moment during Apollo 11 when they deployed the laser ranging retroreflector.

Also nice: tides are slowing Earth; eventually Earth would become tidally locked to the Moon (day = lunar month) but the Sun will die first. So the goodbye will never be completed—the Sun's death interrupts the Moon's departure. Actually as the Sun becomes a red giant, Earth may or may not be engulfed; the Moon's recession will change. There's poignancy: the farewell will never finish.

Also poetic detail: because tides slow the Earth, the Moon drifts away; the energy is conserved—our days lengthen a tiny bit, about 2 milliseconds per century. The day you live is 2 milliseconds longer than the day Shakespeare lived? Actually 2 ms/century means over 400 years about 8 ms—roughly. Could say: the days are getting longer by about two milliseconds every century; leap seconds are the Moon invoicing us for borrowed spin. That's a fun line: leap seconds.

Structure for ~1000 words:
1. Cold open: The Moon is leaving. ~3.8 cm/yr, fingernail rate. (100 words)
2. How we know: Apollo retroreflectors, laser ranging, 2.5-second round trip. (120 words)
3. Why: tides, tidal bulge runs ahead, angular momentum transfer, Earth slows, Moon climbs. Days were shorter; Devonian coral growth bands, ~400 days/year; days lengthen ~2 ms/century; leap seconds as bookkeeping. (180 words)
4. Deep time: young Earth, Moon much closer—huge in the sky, monstrous tides; maybe formation from giant impact, debris. The Moon receding ever since. (120 words)
5. The eclipse coincidence: Sun 400x bigger, 400x farther. Totality: corona, animals confused, temperature drops, the eerie shadow. It's a present-tense coincidence, not a law. (150 words)
6. The expiration: as Moon recedes, annular eclipses already more common; in a few hundred million years, no totality. We live in the window. Analogies: catching a wave, a doorway open briefly. (130 words)
7. Reflection: we assume the sky is the permanent thing and our lives the fleeting ones, but the sky is fleeting too—just on a different clock. The consolation of scale: the window is so long every human who will ever exist may fit inside it. The farewell will never finish—the Sun dies first. Close with something resonant: maybe the image of standing in the umbra, the shadow of a departing body passing over you—the Moon's goodbye touching your face for a few minutes. (200 words)

That totals roughly 1000. 

Let me make sure facts are right:
- Lunar recession: 3.8 cm/year ± 0.07, measured by Apache Point Observatory Lunar Laser-ranging Operation (APOLLO) and earlier McDonald Observatory. Yes.
- Round trip time for laser: distance ~384,400 km average, one way ~1.28 seconds, round trip ~2.56 seconds. Yes.
- Retroreflectors: Apollo 11, 14, 15 (three arrays), plus two French-built reflectors on Soviet Lunokhod 1 and 2 rovers. Apollo 11's was deployed by Buzz Aldrin. Correct.
- Tidal mechanism: Earth rotates faster than Moon orbits, so tidal bulge is carried ahead of the Earth-Moon line; the bulge's gravity pulls the Moon forward in its orbit, adding orbital energy, raising the orbit; reaction torque slows Earth's spin. Yes.
- Devonian corals: growth band analyses suggest ~400 days per year in the Devonian (~370-400 Ma), meaning day length ~21.9 hours. Yes, commonly cited.
- Day lengthening: about 1.7–2.3 ms per century. Commonly cited ~1.8 ms/century from tidal friction alone, but observed against atomic clocks it varies. I can say "about two milliseconds per century" as approximate.
- Leap seconds: 27 leap seconds added since 1972. Earth's rotation variability means leap seconds are actually more about irregularities, but tidal friction is the secular trend. I can phrase carefully: "the reason we occasionally need leap seconds is partly that the planet is being braked by tides."
- Early Earth day: after the Moon-forming impact, day possibly ~4-6 hours. Commonly cited ~6 hours not long after formation; ~4 hours immediately post-impact. I'll say something like "a day on the young Earth may have lasted only six hours."
- Moon formation: giant impact hypothesis, Theia, debris disk. Yes.
- Moon closer early: at ~4.5 Ga the Moon was maybe 20,000-25,000 km away (within Roche-ish constraints it formed just outside Roche limit ~18,000 km). It would have looked enormous. I can say "a few times closer" or "perhaps a tenth of its current distance" — 384,000/25,000 ≈ 15x closer. Safe phrasing: "perhaps a tenth as far away" is conservative-ish but fine if hedged. Maybe say "many times closer" to be safe, with tides hundreds of times stronger (tide scales as 1/r³; at 4x closer tides are 64x stronger; at 15x closer, ~3400x). I'll hedge: "tides hundreds of feet high" — hmm, better to say "titanic tides" without numbers, or "tides that would make our coastal charts look like jokes." Keep it evocative but hedged.
- Sun/Moon angular size: Sun diameter ~1.39 million km, Moon ~3,474 km. Ratio ~400. Sun distance ~150 million km, Moon ~384,000 km; ratio ~390. Yes, the famous coincidence.
- Annular vs total: annular eclipses are actually slightly more frequent than total ones currently (~33% annular, ~27% total, rest partial/hybrid) because of orbital eccentricities. So the coincidence is already fraying—true and poignant.
- When will totality end: estimates ~600 million years (some say 620 million years for last total eclipse, others that perfect total eclipses become rare within 300 My and impossible by ~600-700 My). I'll say "some hundreds of millions of years" or "somewhere around 600 million years" hedged.
- Sun's red giant phase: ~5 billion years. So Sun dies long after totality ends. Wait—for my "farewell never finishes" line: the point was Earth would tidally lock to the Moon only after ~50 billion years, longer than the Sun's remaining life, so the Moon's retreat will stop when the Sun dies. And total eclipses end ~600 My from now, which is also before the Sun's death. The "goodbye never finished" line: the process of the Moon receding and Earth slowing will be interrupted by the Sun's death—Earth might be engulfed or orbit changes. So "the farewell will never be completed; the Sun will go out first" — actually the Sun becomes a red giant, not just goes out; either way, poetic license fine: "the Sun will intervene first."

Hmm wait, sequence check: totality ends ~600 My; red giant ~5 Gy. So eclipses end long before the Sun's death. The line "we'll lose the eclipses while there are still 4.4 billion years of sunlight left" is a nice touch.

Another nice detail: during totality, temperature drops measurably (several degrees), birds go to roost, crickets chirp, horizon glows 360° like sunset in every direction, stars come out at midday, the corona visible. The umbra sweeps across Earth at supersonic speed (thousands of km/h—actually the shadow moves at ~1,700 km/h at the equator up to faster at higher latitudes; Mach 1.5+). Could say "a shadow sweeping across the Earth faster than sound."

Also: only on Earth (as far as we know among well-known examples) do we get this perfect eclipse coincidence—though moons of other planets can occult the Sun from their surfaces; Saturn's moon... eh, skip comparative planetology or one clause.

I want the prose to be genuinely good—rhythmic, precise, a little wry. Let me think about voice: an essayist's voice, first person plural or first person minimal; conversational but with awe. Some short sentences for punch. Avoid purple excess; let facts carry the wonder.

The mirrors still work. Nothing has knocked them over. There is no wind.

Here is the strange part: the Moon is not drifting off due to some lingering recoil from its creation. It is being pushed. And the pusher is us.

The Earth turns once a day; the Moon takes a month to orbit. Because our planet spins faster than its companion circles, the tidal bulge the Moon raises in our oceans gets dragged slightly ahead of the Moon's position. That forward-leaning bulge has gravity, and its gravity tugs on the Moon, giving it a small continuous boost—adding orbital energy, letting it climb to a higher, slower orbit. Every push has a price. The Earth pays in spin: braked by the very tides it flings ahead, our day lengthens by about two milliseconds every century. In effect, the rotational energy of our planet is being handed up to the Moon, dollar by dollar, and the Moon spends it on altitude.

We can check the old ledgers. Certain corals lay down fine daily growth lines within annual bands—a clock inside a calendar. Devonian corals, 370 million years old, record about 400 days per year. The year hasn't changed. The days were shorter, each one about 22 hours long. The Devonian reef-dwellers lived slightly faster lives than we do, in a world spinning slightly quicker beneath them.

Go back further and the Moon crowds the sky. It was likely born in violence—a Mars-sized body striking the young Earth and splashing a ring of debris into orbit, which congealed into the Moon, hovering then at a fraction of its present distance. For a long stretch of deep time it must have hung enormous and low, dragging tides of a scale our coastal charts would treat as satire, over a planet still warm from the collision. It has been climbing away ever since. Four and a half billion years of retreat, and we arrived late enough in the process to think of it as scenery.

And yet we are lucky in a way so specific it feels personal. The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon—and also about 400 times farther away. Geometry therefore performs a small miracle: the two disks match. When the Moon's orbit crosses the Sun's path precisely enough, the Moon covers the Sun exactly, edge to edge, and a shadow sweeps across the Earth faster than sound. Under that shadow the temperature drops, birds go quiet or go home, a strange 360-degree twilight glows on every horizon at once, and the sky's one impossibility appears: the corona, the Sun's outer atmosphere, otherwise invisible, suddenly blazing around a black hole in the day.

This is not a law of physics. It is a coincidence, and it has an expiration date.

Because orbits are ellipses, the Moon is sometimes nearer to us and sometimes farther. When an eclipse occurs while the Moon is on the far side of its range, its disk falls short of the Sun's and we get an annular eclipse—a ring of fire, daylight leaking around the rim. Annular eclipses already slightly outnumber total ones. The average Moon is getting smaller in our sky by the year, at fingernail speed. Somewhere around 600 million years from now, by most estimates, the geometry will fail for good: no more totality, ever. The corona will go unmasked until the Sun itself changes character. Anyone around for the last one will attend an event with no sequel.

We tend to assume the sky is the permanent thing and we are the temporary thing. The Moon's slow exit suggests otherwise. Permanence is a matter of which clock you consult. Mountains are fleeting to geology; species are fleeting to biology; and it turns out even the neat alignments of the heavens are fleeting to astronomy—a limited engagement that happened to be running when we bought our tickets.

But consider the length of the run. Some hundreds of millions of years remain—long enough, probably, to hold every human life that will ever be lived, with seats to spare. No one who reads this, and no one who descends from anyone who reads this, need check the Moon's ticket for expiration. The window is so wide it functions, for all human purposes, as a permanent feature. We live inside a coincidence the way fish live inside water: unaware, and unharmed by the fact that the water, too, is technically leaving.

There is something oddly tender in the mechanism itself. The Moon recedes because the Earth embraces it—because our spinning world seizes the tides and hurls them ahead, and the Moon, receiving the gift, rises. We slow down so that it can climb. The departure is not theft from outside; it is an exchange between the two oldest partners in this neighborhood.

So stand in the path of totality once, if you can manage it. You will be standing inside the Moon's goodbye as it passes over your upturned face—a shadow cast by something leaving, at a speed you will never feel. It has been taking its leave for four billion years, and it is nowhere near done. Indeed, the farewell will never be completed; long before the Moon finishes going, the Sun will bring the whole scene to a close. The goodbye will be interrupted—which may be the kindest way for anything to end: still in progress, still exactly covering the light, when the lights go out.

Because our planet spins faster than its companion circles, the tidal bulge the Moon raises in our oceans gets dragged slightly ahead of the Moon's position. That forward-leaning bulge has gravity, and its gravity tugs on the Moon, giving it a small continuous boost—adding orbital energy, letting it climb to a higher, slower orbit. Every push has a price. The Earth pays in spin: braked by the very tides it flings ahead, our day lengthens by about two milliseconds every century. In effect, the rotational energy of our planet is being handed up to the Moon, dollar by dollar, and the Moon spends it on altitude.

We can check the old ledgers. Certain corals lay down fine daily growth lines within annual bands—a clock inside a calendar. Devonian corals, 370 million years old, record about 400 days per year. The year hasn't changed. The days were shorter, each one about 22 hours long. The Devonian reef-dwellers lived slightly faster lives than we do, in a world spinning slightly quicker beneath them.

Go back further and the Moon crowds the sky. It was likely born in violence—a Mars-sized body striking the young Earth and splashing a ring of debris into orbit, which congealed into the Moon, hovering then at a fraction of its present distance. For a long stretch of deep time it must have hung enormous and low, dragging tides of a scale our coastal charts would treat as satire, over a planet still warm from the collision. It has been climbing away ever since. Four and a half billion years of retreat, and we arrived late enough in the process to think of it as scenery.

And yet we are lucky in a way so specific it feels personal. The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon—and also about 400 times farther away. Geometry therefore performs a small miracle: the two disks match. When the Moon's orbit crosses the Sun's path precisely enough, the Moon covers the Sun exactly, edge to edge, and a shadow sweeps across the Earth faster than sound. Under that shadow the temperature drops, birds go quiet or go home, a strange 360-degree twilight glows on every horizon at once, and the sky's one impossibility appears: the corona, the Sun's outer atmosphere, otherwise invisible, suddenly blazing around a black hole in the day.

This is not a law of physics. It is a coincidence, and it has an expiration date.

Because orbits are ellipses, the Moon is sometimes nearer to us and sometimes farther. When an eclipse occurs while the Moon is on the far side of its range, its disk falls short of the Sun's and we get an annular eclipse—a ring of fire, daylight leaking around the rim. Annular eclipses already slightly outnumber total ones. The average Moon is getting smaller in our sky by the year, at fingernail speed. Somewhere around 600 million years from now, by most estimates, the geometry will fail for good: no more totality, ever. The corona will go unmasked until the Sun itself changes character. Anyone around for the last one will attend an event with no sequel.

We tend to assume the sky is the permanent thing and we are the temporary thing. The Moon's slow exit suggests otherwise. Permanence is a matter of which clock you consult. Mountains are fleeting to geology; species are fleeting to biology; and it turns out even the neat alignments of the heavens are fleeting to astronomy—a limited engagement that happened to be running when we bought our tickets.

But consider the length of the run. Some hundreds of millions of years remain—long enough, probably, to hold every human life that will ever be lived, with seats to spare. No one who reads this, and no one who descends from anyone who reads this, need check the Moon's ticket for expiration. The window is so wide it functions, for all human purposes, as a permanent feature. We live inside a coincidence the way fish live inside water: unaware, and unharmed by the fact that the water, too, is technically leaving.

There is something oddly tender in the mechanism itself. The Moon recedes because the Earth embraces it—because our spinning world seizes the tides and hurls them ahead, and the Moon, receiving the gift, rises. We slow down so that it can climb. The departure is not theft from outside; it is an exchange between the two oldest partners in this neighborhood.

So stand in the path of totality once, if you can manage it. You will be standing inside the Moon's goodbye as it passes over your upturned face—a shadow cast by something leaving, at a speed you will never feel. It has been taking its leave for four billion years, and it is nowhere near done. Indeed, the farewell will never be completed; long before the Moon finishes going, the Sun will bring the whole scene to a close. The goodbye will be interrupted—which may be the kindest way for anything to end: still in progress, still exactly covering the light, when the lights go out.
